Hyperledger Fabric Graph Isomorphism Network for Conflict Transactions Detection in

Multi-Version Concurrency Control

![](data:image/png;base64,) **ABSTRACT** Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) is a critical mechanism in blockchain systems such as Hyperledger Fabric. MVCC is crucial for managing concurrent transactions ensuring integrity through versioning and timestamp techniques. Enhancing MVCC is essential due to the significant over- head involved in maintaining multiple versions of data and resolving conflict transactions, particularly in enterprise blockchain applications where data integrity and system reliability are of utmost importance. Conflict transactions are the predominant cause of transaction failures in Hyperledger Fabric where multiple transactions attempt to update data items based on outdated data versions. This study introduces the Hyperledger Fabric-based Modified Graph Isomorphism Network (HFGIN). Employing advanced graph neural networks, HFGIN utilizes node and edge data representations within a graph-based framework, which significantly increases the efficiency of detecting MVCC conflicts. The proposed model aims to detect conflict transactions at an earlier stage in Hyperledger Fabric blockchain systems. Evaluation results indicate that HFGIN substantially outperforms baseline models such as the Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) and Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN). HFGIN achieves a test accuracy of 82.20%, demonstrating a 14.67% improvement over GCN and a 4.12% improvement over GIN. Moreover, HFGIN records a precision of 86.06%, marking an 8.97% enhancement over GCN and 9.46% over GIN. It also shows a recall of 79.56%, which is 17.03% higher than GCN and 1.39% greater than GIN, besides an F1 score improvement of 23.37% over GCN and 5.27% over GIN. HFGIN also demonstrates computational efficiency with low inference latency and minimal resource usage and maintains scalability when tested under larger transaction loads. The model achieves these improvements while maintaining computational efficiency and system scalability by applying inference selectively and enabling parallel execution of non-conflicting transactions. The enhancements contribute to detection rate increase of conflict transactions over GCN and GIN in an earlier stage, demonstrating the model’s potential to transform MVCC conflict management in high-demand blockchain environments such as banking operations.

1. **INTRODUCTION**

Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) is an essen- tial component in modern blockchain systems such as

![](data:image/png;base64,)The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Prakasam Periasamy .

Hyperledger Fabric that are designed for enterprise use. MVCC helps manage concurrent access to the blockchain ledger, ensuring data consistency and isolation among trans- actions by allowing multiple versions of a data item to coexist. The concurrency control mechanism is vital for permissioned blockchains where transaction efficiency and data integrity

are paramount [\[1\]. In](#_bookmark76) blockchain systems, MVCC operates by assigning timestamps or version numbers to each transaction. When a transaction reads data, it accesses the version that was committed before the transaction started, ensuring a consistent view of data. Such versioning allows the system to detect conflicts among concurrent transactions by checking if another transaction has modified the data after the cur- rent transaction’s timestamp. If such a conflict is detected, the transaction can be aborted, thus preventing potential inconsistencies [\[2\].](#_bookmark77)

While effective, MVCC is not without challenges in the context of blockchain. One of the main issues is the overhead associated with maintaining multiple versions of data, which directly affects both storage and processing performance, particularly under high transaction loads. Studies have shown that as the size of the read/write sets grows, MVCC vali- dation time increases significantly, reaching over 750 ms in some cases, especially when CouchDB is used as the state database backend [\[3\].](#_bookmark78) Additionally, the complexity of resolv- ing conflict transactions demands innovative solutions [\[4\].](#_bookmark79) In permissioned blockchains such as Hyperledger Fabric, enhancements to MVCC mechanisms have been explored to improve the efficiency of concurrency control. Such improve- ments include optimizing transaction execution pathways and integrating advanced data structures to manage versions more effectively. For example, Hyperledger Fabric uses an execute- order-validate (EOV) architecture for transaction processing, which allows for greater flexibility and scalability in handling MVCC. The architecture decouples transaction execution from consensus and leverages fine-grained access control over transaction execution, which can help minimize conflicts and improve system performance [\[1\].](#_bookmark76)

Since the advent of Bitcoin, blockchain technology has evolved significantly, leading to the development of various blockchain types, including public and private blockchains. Among the private or permissioned blockchains, Hyper- ledger Fabric stands out due to its modular architecture and pluggable consensus mechanism. Hyperledger Fabric is part of the broader Hyperledger project, which offers mul- tiple frameworks and tools aimed at enhancing blockchain implementations across different sectors [\[5\].](#_bookmark80) Blockchain technology, defined as a distributed ledger technology, facili- tates the verification and approval of transactions of digital assets across a large peer-to-peer network. Its immutable nature ensures that transactions are recorded chronologi- cally in blocks. Every participant in the network shares and simultaneously updates copies of the blockchain, requiring consensus among parties to alter the ledger. Hyperledger Fabric processes transactions based on the EOV mechanism, which ensures transactions are either validated and com- mitted successfully or identified as invalid and aborted [\[6\].](#_bookmark81) One crucial aspect of ensuring the consistency of the ledger in Hyperledger Fabric is the implementation of the MVCC mechanism. MVCC is crucial in maintaining ledger con- sistency and preventing issues such as the double-spending problem. It involves version control to ensure that the state of

the ledger remains unchanged from its initial execution to the final commitment [\[7\].](#_bookmark82)

However, despite such mechanisms, invalid transactions, particularly those arising from conflicts, significantly affect Fabric’s performance. Studies have reported that 40% of failed transactions are due to conflict transactions during the MVCC validation phase [\[8\],](#_bookmark83) [\[9\].](#_bookmark84) Such conflicts typically arise when multiple transactions simultaneously attempt to update the same data element, leading to potential inconsis- tencies and failures [\[8\],](#_bookmark83) [\[10\].](#_bookmark85) The high incidence of conflict transactions in Hyperledger Fabric underscores a significant challenge: the need for more efficient conflict detection and resolution mechanisms. Current strategies, while effective to a degree, still allow a substantial number of conflicts to affect the system’s efficiency and reliability adversely. This study highlights the critical need for research into opti- mized solutions that can enhance MVCC conflict detection in blockchain systems, particularly in environments as complex and widely used as Hyperledger Fabric.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**FIGURE 1.** Early stage conflict detection in the EOV process using HFGIN.

The objective of this research is to develop a novel Graph Isomorphism Network-based model, specifically customized for Hyperledger Fabric, that can detect MVCC conflicts earlier and with greater accuracy than current models. The model, termed the Hyperledger Fabric-based Modified Graph Isomorphism Network (HFGIN), is designed to integrate with the existing EOV framework of Hyperledger Fabric.

The main contribution of this research is to enhance the detection rate and reduce conflict transaction detection time in Hyperledger Fabric in an early stage of EOV. HFGIN reduces the time and computational overhead associated with conflict resolution by initiating conflict detection at the ear- liest point of transaction processing as shown in Figure [1](#_bookmark11) instead of validation stage. The study sets a baseline in early conflict detection in permissioned framework blockchain sys- tems based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). It is an

essential contribution towards enhancing the reliability of blockchain technology in enterprise systems with high trans- action volumes, where data integrity plays a crucial role.

This paper is structured as follows. Section [II](#_bookmark12) discusses related work. Section [III](#_bookmark40) details the methodology. Section [IV](#_bookmark55) presents implementation of the proposal, experiments, and evaluation. Finally, Section [V](#_bookmark74) concludes the work.

1. **RELATED WORK**
   1. _MVCC IN BLOCKCHAIN_

MVCC is an essential technology in blockchain systems, particularly for platforms such as Hyperledger Fabric, which cater to enterprise applications. MVCC’s primary role in blockchain is to ensure data consistency by allowing trans- actions to operate on multiple versions of data, thus ensuring a stable and consistent view even amidst concurrent updates. It enhances data integrity and stabilizes the blockchain’s oper- ational framework, crucial in sectors where high data fidelity is mandatory [\[9\],](#_bookmark84) [\[11\].](#_bookmark86) However, implementing MVCC in blockchain environments comes with its set of challenges. Traditionally, the primary concern has been the performance overhead associated with managing multiple data versions, which can significantly affect transaction processing speeds as system demands escalate [\[12\].](#_bookmark87) Additionally, maintaining the versions demands substantial storage and computational resources, compounding operational costs and system com- plexity [\[13\].](#_bookmark88) The decentralized nature of blockchain adds another layer of complexity to MVCC, especially concerning concurrency control and conflict resolution. In a blockchain, synchronization of state across all nodes, devoid of any cen- tral authority, is required, which complicates the consistency of data versions across the distributed ledger [\[14\].](#_bookmark89) More- over, timely detection and resolution of conflicts are critical; delays in addressing such issues can lead to decreased system performance [\[9\]](#_bookmark84) where it is still extremely less capable in transaction processing than decentralized systems such as Visa [\[5\],](#_bookmark80) [\[15\],](#_bookmark90) [\[16\].](#_bookmark91)

Recent advancements in blockchain technology have encouraged research into more efficient ways of handling MVCC challenges. Innovations such as optimized data structures for version management and the use of smart contracts for automated conflict resolution are among the solutions being explored to improve MVCC’s efficiency within blockchain systems [\[17\].](#_bookmark92)

- 1. _REVIEW OF CONFLICT DETECTION METHODS_

Increasing transactions processing improvement in Hyper- ledger Fabric has been researched recently. However, only a few works have concentrated on conflict transactions detection issues [\[19\].](#_bookmark93) The primary cause of conflicts is the interdependence of two transactions that simultaneously access and modify the same key version, where one updates while the other reads the key simultaneously. Therefore, some researchers have analyzed the dependencies to iden- tify the conflicts. Generally, there are two main approaches,

reordering mechanism, and cache mechanism, in addressing the conflict transactions in Hyperledger Fabric [\[20\].](#_bookmark94) Reorder- ing mechanism involves mainly graph-based dependency analysis. It produces a conflict graph (a cyclic graph) of all the transactions in a specific block based on the read-set and write-set (RW set) of the transactions.

1. REORDERING BASED APPROACHES

Fabric++ is introduced by the researchers in [\[21\]](#_bookmark95) which removes the locking mechanism used by Hyperledger Fabric but terminates transactions prematurely that involve reading

data across blocks. By building a conflict graph that repre- sents transactions dependencies, all cycles can be identified in the graph using Tarjan’s and Johnson’s algorithms. It then removes the transactions that occur in the most cycles, greed- ily, until all cycles are resolved obtaining an acyclic graph.

FabricSharp in the study [\[22\]](#_bookmark96) uses snapshots to ensure that the data read by a transaction is consistent across blocks. FabricSharp implements a fine-grained concurrency control method. The solution suggests that transaction reorder- ing is not effective in some cases such as if there is a committed transaction in the dependencies which makes reordering impossible because of blockchain immutability. Therefore, they are identified and the unorderable transac- tions are removed to allow only serializable transactions to be reordered.

Both Fabric++ and FabricSharp generate a conflict graph to represent transactions dependency for conflict detection. The difference is that dependencies graph in Fabric++ rep- resents transactions in the same block only as the algorithm

works on graph that represents only transactions of a block, therefore, it can deal with intra block MVCC read conflicts only while FabricSharp generates the graph across blocks and handles both inter and intra block conflict transactions.

The researchers in [\[23\]](#_bookmark97) proposed a modified system of Fabric++. The modified system is known as FabricUp which uses the key-value pair of the transaction in the validation phase to detect the conflict transactions, based on the same

cyclic graph as in Fabric++. However, instead of generating a serialization after identifying the cyclic conflict graph of

conflict transaction, FabricUp decomposes the graphs into an acyclic graph and returns a failure signal to the client without waiting for a timeout error such as in Fabric++. Then, the client initiates a second proposal after receiving the failure signal and the system generates a serializable transaction

sequence based on the remaining transactions. Both systems Fabric++ and FabricUp only deal with intra-block conflict transactions.

The researchers in [\[20\]](#_bookmark94) proposed CATPFabric that uses key-based transaction grouping algorithm (based on RW sets) to enable highly parallel processing of conflicting transac- tions. Then the Group ID is used to divide the transactions into several groups based on the version number, where lower version numbers are filtered out and only the highest version numbers are stored. Transaction retransmission is

reduced by reordering the read-only transactions till they are successfully validated and committed. Used all read-only transactions to handle them first can ensure that all read-only transactions can be committed successfully in the validation phase, thereby reducing the number of transaction retrans- missions. Although CATP-Fabric can successfully handle almost all transactions in the case of high concurrency con- flict and achieves significantly better performance for IoT applications, it suffers from issues related to the reordering

mechanism similar to Fabric++.

1. CACHE BASED MECHANISMS

Using cache mechanisms, there are different techniques to detect conflict transactions in Hyperledger Fabric. It is the most used mechanism for solving the concurrent transaction issues in Hyperledger Fabric.

The authors in [\[24\]](#_bookmark98) studied transaction isolation in Hyper- ledger Fabric. The study argues that the locking mechanism of Hyperledger Fabric is a major performance setback for the system, due to the locking of the entire state database during simulation of transactions. Therefore, the authors proposed a lockfree mechanism to utilize the intrinsic versioning of the keys in the state database, which are primarily used to perform the MVCC check during the validation phase. Thus, along with the readily existing save point mechanism, such lock-free mechanism generates a clear reflection of the world state of transaction for the simulation.

The researchers [\[15\]](#_bookmark90) proposed a blockchain machine, a hardware accelerator integrated with a specified commu- nication protocol, to act as validation peer in the Hyper- ledger Fabric. The proposed blockchain machine collects the blocks and the associated transaction records directly in the CPU from the network interface and then validates the transactions by a block-level and transaction-level pipeline. To detect the conflict transaction, the authors used conven- tional MVCC protocols existing in the Hyperledger Fabric to check read-write conflicts between the transactions.

FabricCRDT is introduced by the researchers in [\[7\]](#_bookmark82) which is based on the control-free replicated datatypes that allow node replicas to converge to a consistent state without los- ing updates. The system can resolve all types of conflict transactions. The system merges the key values of the con- flicting transactions by using CRDT techniques before being committed to the ledger. Then, the merged CRDT object is converted into a byte array that replaces the value of the key-value pair in the write-set of the transaction. This approach successfully separates all the conflicting transac- tions and discards them before validation.

XOX Fabric is proposed by the research work [\[25\].](#_bookmark99) The author focused on the intra-block concurrent conflicts. XOX- Fabric employs a tool called the ‘‘transaction dependency analyzer’’ that identifies dependencies between transactions by tracking all accesses to keys by the generated RW sets. If the analyzer identifies a dependency on an earlier trans- action, that transaction is invalidated during Fabric’s RW set validation and then executed again in a next step using the

latest world state which can resolve any conflicts that arose after the first execution. There is no implementation report for this solution to be analyzed. The concurrency conflicts are reduced significantly due to the lack of knowledge of con- current transactions during pre-order execution. However, the system has a tradeoff between concurrent high-performance execution and consistent linear execution.

The researchers in [\[16\]](#_bookmark91) studied the performance and scala- bility issues in Hyperledger Fabric. The authors observed that during horizontal scaling, redundant workloads across the nodes waste computational resources while during vertical scaling, virtual-CPU remains underused. Thus, the authors proposed SmartFabric based on new nodes, called sparse nodes, based on the sharding concept in distributed databases. In order to detect the dependency among transactions, the system used Read-Write Trie, where the state values are stored in internal nodes and references to the transactions are stored in the leaf nodes. The system uses GetNextTrans- action() operation to validate the transactions until the later transaction has no out-edges in the dependency graph. How- ever, there is high latency during scaling down of the sparse peers. As a result, [\[20\]](#_bookmark94) pointed out that since the IoT devices are delay sensitive, conflict transactions are significantly higher.

Additionally, TimeFabric was proposed by the study [\[26\]](#_bookmark100) to validate client-assigned transaction timestamps. TimeFab- ric assigns a tamper-resistant timestamp to each block and the timestamps can be used by the blockchain network for the deterministic smart contract execution. It detects concurrent conflicts by applying GetHistoryRangeForKey() operation. The read set of the transaction contains all the keys cache and state database for the auditability of the data. In the validation phase of the TimeFabric, it only validates the key reads from the state database, while the cache database is never updated. Thus, this approach reduces the concurrency conflicts. How- ever, the system produces lower throughput, since widely distributed nodes may result in failed endorsements.

FabricETP detects the inter block and intra block conflict types in the ordering service and validation phase respec- tively [\[10\].](#_bookmark85) Inter block conflicts are identified by comparing the key version of received transactions key to the version of the same key in a cache-based database. Those conflicts

are required to be resubmitted again after FabricETP inval- idates them. Using the Tarjan algorithm as in Fabric++, a conflict graph is constructed. Additionally, it involves other techniques from graph theory such as random walk for the

intra block conflicts detection. The study in [\[9\]](#_bookmark84) implemented a cache mechanism to abort the intra block conflicts only in the executing phase. It requires a specific environment such as using the AND endorsement policy for a good performance.

- 1. _GRAPH THEORY AND BLOCKCHAIN_

The integration of graph-based approaches in network analy- sis has significantly enhanced the modelling and visualiza- tion of complex data interactions within various networks,

including social, biological, and technological infrastruc- tures. In blockchain technology, such methodologies have been increasingly recognized for their potential to man- age and analyze the complex web of transactions that define blockchain systems. The representation of transac- tions as nodes and the interactions as edges in a graph facilitates detailed insights into transaction patterns, which is crucial for detecting anomalies and optimizing system performance [\[27\].](#_bookmark101) Graph-based models are effective in envi- ronments dominated by inter-node relationships, such as blockchain, where they can improve security by identifying fraudulent patterns or optimize mining strategies through the analysis of transaction connectivity [\[28\].](#_bookmark102) Moreover, such approaches contribute to scalability enhancements by iden- tifying bottlenecks in transaction processing networks [\[27\].](#_bookmark101) Graph theory is also applied to refine consensus mechanisms, which are essential for validating transactions and achieving agreement on their chronological order. Such application helps create more robust blockchain architectures, essential for handling increasing transaction volumes as blockchain applications expand [\[29\].](#_bookmark103)

Furthermore, graph-based techniques are essential in advancing blockchain’s concurrency control mechanisms, such as MVCC [\[9\]. It](#_bookmark84) is possible to manage data versions across the blockchain more efficiently by mapping transac- tions and their dependencies into a graph, ensuring ledger integrity and consistency, particularly in high-demand enter- prise applications. Figure [2](#_bookmark33) illustrates the application of graph-based techniques to facilitate blockchain concurrency control mechanisms such as MVCC. Such approach enhances the management of data versions within the blockchain by mapping transactions and their dependencies into a graphical representation. Each node in the graph represents a distinct version of data, while edges indicate the interactions or trans- actions that modify or access these versions. Figure [2](#_bookmark33) depicts the way MVCC can be leveraged to maintain ledger integrity and consistency by clearly representing the relationships between various data versions and transactions. It represents a model of transaction interaction within blockchain system using MVCC, illustrates a network of nodes, each represent- ing a version of data (V1 to V10) and directed edges that denote transactions operations (read or write). For instance, transaction T1 reads from V1, and transaction T2 reads from V2, indicating the flow of data access. Transactions such as T3 not only read from V4 but also write to V5, showing how one transaction might interact with multiple data versions. The graph helps in understanding how MVCC maintains data integrity and consistency by managing the versions and transactions efficiently. Such a graph-based model is crucial for high-demand enterprise applications, where the efficient management of data versions and transaction dependencies is crucial to ensure operational reliability and accuracy. Hyperledger Fabric Blockchain systems can better handle the complexities of concurrent data access and modifications by employing graph-based techniques, thus optimizing overall performance.

Graphs possess expressive power for complex data struc- ture and can be infused with machine learning. GNNs are the most preferred option when it comes to learning algo- rithms applied to graph data since they offer the potential to incorporate neighborhood information within a comprehen- sive learning approach [\[30\].](#_bookmark104) Empirical evidence supports the effectiveness of GNNs, as they have consistently achieved state-of-the-art performance in node classification, link pre- diction, and graph classification [\[31\].](#_bookmark105)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**FIGURE 2.** Blockchain MVCC transactions network graph.

Their exceptional performance in these domains has sur- prised other existing methods, establishing GNNs as a powerful tool for extracting meaningful insights and making accurate predictions from graph-structured data. Graph Con- volutional Networks (GCNs) have been a groundbreaking innovation that was developed to analyze data structured as graphs. Introduced by Kipf and Welling in their influen- tial 2016 paper, GCNs adapt the principles of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to graph data. GCNs enable the extraction of features directly from the graph structure [\[32\].](#_bookmark106) GCNs mitigate the challenge of applying neural network methodologies to graph data by incorporating the idea of neighbourhood aggregation. Blockchain technology has adopted GNNs to address various challenges and setbacks such as detecting identity inference [\[33\],](#_bookmark107) fraud [\[34\],](#_bookmark108) anomaly detection [\[35\],](#_bookmark109) and account classification [\[36\].](#_bookmark110)

The most expressive GNN from the literature is Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) according to [\[31\].](#_bookmark105) The authors argue that if the aggregation scheme of a GNN, such as GIN, is able to capture injective functions (i.e., unique map- pings), it can achieve the same discriminative power as the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) graph isomorphism test [\[37\],](#_bookmark111) a well-known algorithm used for graph comparison. There- fore, the aggregation part is the most important part to improve the expressiveness of GNN. The aggregation is con- ducted on the neighboring nodes. The GIN is a significant achievement in the area of graph-based deep learning, which offers a powerful model for learning graph representations

that capture the complexities of graph structures and node features effectively. It was developed to address the limita- tions of earlier GCNs, GIN has demonstrated efficiency at distinguishing different graph structures, a task that is crucial in applications ranging from chemical compound analysis to social network modelling [\[31\].](#_bookmark105) The GIN model is powerful in capturing the complexities of graph structures, it, however, falls short in transaction dependency representation required for MVCC conflict detection. GIN does not inherently aggre- gate edge features, such as the types of dependencies among transactions, write-read (w-r), read-write (r-w), and write- write (w-w). Such transaction interactions are crucial for accurately predicting conflicts as they highlight the direc- tional and relational complexities between transactions that could potentially lead to conflict transactions. To enhance GIN’s applicability in detecting MVCC conflicts, it is nec- essary to modify the aggregation functions to incorporate edge features along with node features. The modification would enable GIN to effectively process different types of transaction dependencies, improving its predictive accuracy and utility in complex transactional environments.

1. **METHODOLOGY**
   1. _SMALLBANK CHAINCODE_

Bitcoin [\[38\]](#_bookmark112) represents the first widely recognized applica- tion of blockchain technology, enabling cryptocurrency trans- actions such as transfers and payments directly between users without the involvement of intermediaries. Subsequently, various other blockchain-based applications have emerged, including cryptocurrencies such as Ethereum, which allows developers to create smart contracts. Smart contracts are self-executing agreements with terms written directly within the code.

SmallBank chaincode simulates banking operations by executing six types of operations, TransactSavings, DepositChecking, SendPayment, WriteCheck, Amalgamate, and Query. SmallBank is not only used to evaluate concurrent conflict transactions of centralized systems such as [\[39\],](#_bookmark113) but also it is used to benchmark many proposed solutions for concurrent conflict transactions in blockchain such as [\[21\]](#_bookmark95) and [\[22\].](#_bookmark96)

Furthermore, SmallBank was used by the researchers in [\[40\]](#_bookmark114) as a representative workload for financial banking to evaluate the scalability and applicability of the Quorum blockchain and its consensus algorithms. Therefore, Small- Bank chaincode is considered suitable for banking operations workload simulation in blockchain systems.

- 1. _DATA COLLECTION_

The conflict and non-conflict transactions can be generated by executing the operations in SmallBank chaincode and changing the skewness of user accounts access. In Fabric- Sharp [\[22\] a](#_bookmark96) Workload Generator function was created to generate the transactions in the blockchain blocks based on SmallBank chaincode. The function includes all transaction

types. The workload consists of 10,000 accounts with Zipfian distribution adjusted to control the skewness. The Zipfian is adjusted from 0 to 1.2 in steps of 0.2, to control the access. In Fabric++ [\[21\],](#_bookmark95) 100,000 accounts are created with random balances and two account types for each user. Zipfian distri-

bution varies from 0 to 2 to control the skewness of accessed accounts. Both workloads are configured to distribute Small- Bank transaction executions with different Zipfian skewness values of accessed accounts for conflict and non-conflict transactions generation.

In this experiment, the same function is used to create 10,000 accounts representing the customer’s account and populated with the value 1,000,000 for each saving and checking balances, increasing number from 1 to 10,000 as account id values of the created accounts, and ‘User’

\+ ‘increasingNumber’ as the value of the created account names. The Zipfian distribution is adjusted to a higher

value to create conflict transactions as well as non-conflict transactions as equal as possible. Therefore, the Zipfian dis- tribution in the workloadGenerator code is adjusted to 1.6 for account access skewness to generate non-conflict and conflict transactions. The transaction type can be picked randomly from SmallBank chaincode to be run over the selected hot accounts. All the transactions are fired by 2 different peers resulting in 1995 transactions.

To further assess the scalability of the proposed approach in real-world large-scale environments, we extended the simu- lation beyond the original 1,995-transaction setup. As shown in Table [1](#_bookmark44), additional experiments were conducted using 3,000 and 5,000 transactions while proportionally increas- ing the number of accounts to maintain key diversity and avoid artificial saturation. The Zipfian skewness factor was retained at 1.6 to simulate a moderately skewed access pattern representative of enterprise scenarios with a mix of conflict and non-conflict transactions. This extended setup provided a denser and more complex workload suitable for evaluating scalability. The goal was to analyze how increasing transac- tion volume affects conflict density, graph size, construction time, and memory utilization. The generated datasets under these higher loads were used to perform detailed large-scale performance profiling, with specific emphasis on transaction conflict graph growth and its impact on GNN training and inference.

To further validate the robustness of the proposed model across varying access patterns, we extended the dataset gen- eration by incorporating Zipfian skewness values of 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, and 1.8. These distributions represent increasing levels of contention, with lower skewness depicting more uniform access and higher skewness emphasizing hotspot access pat- terns typical in financial workloads. Such variation allows us to investigate the generalization performance of HFGIN under diverse conflict densities. While the SmallBank bench- mark remains the central workload due to its relevance in simulating financial operations and its widespread adoption in concurrency control research, the inclusion of Zipfian diversity strengthens the experimental rigor and simulates

- 1. _DATA PREPROCESSING_

Data preprocessing is a crucial step in preparing the raw blockchain transaction data for analysis and model training. The dataset used in this study consists of various attributes

detailing each transaction, including the ‘read_set’ and ‘write_set’ fields comprising JSON-like structures. Such fields contain essential information about the operations per- formed during each transaction. The preprocessing begins with parsing the JSON-like structures to extract meaning- ful data. It involves developing custom parsing functions to interpret the nested information within the ‘read_set’ and ‘write_set’ fields. The primary goal is to convert such complex structures into a more manageable tabular format that can be easily analyzed. The dataset is then cleaned by handling any missing or inconsistent values to ensure data integrity. The step also includes the conversion of timestamp data into a standardized format, allowing for temporal analysis. Furthermore, categorical variables, such as ‘validation_code’, are encoded into numerical val- ues to facilitate their use in machine learning models. The comprehensive preprocessing step ensures that the dataset is well-structured, consistent, and ready for subsequent feature extraction and normalization processes.

- 1. _FEATURE EXTRACTION_

Feature extraction is an essential process to transform the raw, preprocessed data into meaningful numerical represen- tations that can be used for model training. In this study, we focus on extracting features from the ‘read_set’ and ‘write_set’ fields of the blockchain transactions. The fields contain details about the keys accessed during each transaction. The custom parsing functions developed during preprocessing count the number of keys in the set arrays of both ‘read_set’ and ‘write_set’. It results in two new features, ‘num_keys_read’ and ‘num_keys_write’, which represent the number of keys accessed during read and write operations, respectively. Such features provide cru- cial insights into the transaction activities and are indicative of potential conflicts when multiple transactions attempt to access the same keys simultaneously. The rationale behind this approach is the central role such sets play in the genesis and resolution of MVCC conflicts within blockchain sys- tems. By design, read and write sets include all necessary versioning information of data items accessed during transac- tions processing, making them direct indicators of potential dependencies discrepancies that could lead to transaction conflicts. This focus streamlines the computational process by reducing complexity and enhancing the efficiency of the model and aligns closely with the core mechanism operation. Such an approach ensures that the model is optimized for performance and is precise in targeting the most relevant data for conflict detection. The specificity significantly min- imizes the incidence of false positives and false negatives, thereby improving the reliability of the system. Addition- ally, the method mirrors the validation protocols already in place within the last stage of blockchain architectures such as Hyperledger Fabric, which rely on such sets to enforce data consistency and integrity during transactions validation. Additionally, we extract other relevant features such as the transaction’s block ID, timestamp, and validation status. Such

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**FIGURE 4.** Distribution of ‘num_keys_read’ and ‘num_keys_write’ before and after normalization.

features collectively form a rich dataset that captures the essential aspects of each transaction, enabling them to build robust predictive models for conflict detection.

In addition to extracting scalar features such as ‘num_keys_read’ and ‘num_keys_write’, the pro- posed model extensively utilizes the transaction conflict graph structure described in the subsequent sections. Each node in this graph corresponds to a transaction, and edges between nodes capture detailed dependency relationships such as read-write, write-read, and write-write conflicts, along with temporal and control dependencies. These edge relationships are used for graph construction and are actively integrated into the node update mechanisms of the HFGIN model. Specifically, edge features are concatenated with node embeddings during the message-passing process in each convolutional layer, as defined in Equation [3](#_bookmark48). It enables the model to encode the identity of adjacent transactions and the nature and directionality of their interactions, which is crucial for accurately detecting MVCC conflicts.

The diversity of node types, including timestamp nodes, read/write nodes, and static minor nodes, enables the model to encode a rich representation of each transaction’s contextual and structural role in the blockchain network. Timestamp nodes, for instance, allow the model to factor in temporal ordering constraints, while hash nodes model inter-block dependencies, supporting inter-block conflict identification. Moreover, control edges connecting metadata such as user balance or chaincode identifiers to transaction activity nodes help represent the internal logic of transactional behavior beyond superficial key-level interactions. The model gains a more general and expressive understanding of transaction dynamics by integrating both node-level attributes and edge- level relationships. Such graph representation enables the network to learn complex patterns that might otherwise be lost in flattened or tabular formats, thereby improving conflict detection performance beyond what scalar features alone can achieve. Such a design enhances the model’s capacity

to generalize across diverse conflict scenarios in real-world blockchain environments.

- 1. _NORMALISATION_

Following the extraction of key features, normalization is applied to ensure that these features can be effectively utilized in predictive modelling without bias due to scale discrep- ancies. It is an essential step in preparing the extracted features for machine learning models, ensuring that all fea- tures contribute equally to the model’s learning process. In this study, the extracted numerical features, particularly ‘num_keys_read’ and ‘num_keys_write’, are nor- malized using the StandardScaler method. The technique standardizes data by removing the mean and scaling it to unit variance, transforming the features to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. The normalization pro- cess mitigates the impact of differing scales among features, which can adversely affect model performance. Histograms and violin plots depicted in Figure [4](#_bookmark46) are used to compare the distribution of the features before and after normalization. Histograms reveal the concentration and spread of values, showing how normalization centers the data around zero. Vio- lin plots provide a more detailed view of the data distribution, highlighting the density and variability. The plots confirm that normalization effectively standardized feature scales, ensuring that the machine learning models can now process data efficiently and accurately. Normalization enhances the model’s ability to learn from the data by converting the features to a common scale. It improves the overall reliability of the conflict detection system in Hyperledger Fabric.

- 1. _TRANSACTION CONFLICT GRAPH_

The data was prepared for graph-based analysis. It involved developing nodes for each transaction along with special- ized nodes for each timestamp, read, and write operation as extracted from the transaction data. Edges were included to

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**FIGURE 5.** Blockchain transaction conflict graph.

connect each transaction node to its respective read and write nodes, as well as the timestamp nodes, which indicate the flow and dependencies between the data. Such an approach is very clear and instrumental for the application of GNNs, which are efficient in learning from and making predictions on conflict patterns around blockchain transactions based on graph data.

The dataset columns such as ‘blockid’, ‘id’, ‘validation_code’, ‘createdt’, ‘read_set’, and ‘write_set’, exhibit the dynamics involved in represen- tation of the transactions in blockchain. The initial step is to load the dataset from an excel file into pandas DataFrame. Secondly, the previous step is thoroughly observed in order to comprehend the structure, data types, and data completeness. Missing or null values in critical columns are assigned with appropriate defaults or by deleting the inadequate rows. The ‘createdt’ column, containing the transaction timestamps, is converted to a pandas datetime format to assist in more accurate temporal analysis. The next step is the parsing of JSON-like strings of the ‘read_set’ and ‘write_set’ columns to create structured lists or dictionaries. The step is essential towards the processing of the raw data to a form that can be used for graph generation. Since the dataset is significantly large, and for the reasons of performance, just a subsample of 100 transactions is randomly selected for the visualization process.

In the process of construction of the graph, each transac- tion is represented by **key nodes** of various types, read set (Kr), write set (Kw), and timestamp (Kt). The edges among the key nodes represent the read-write/write-read depen-

dencies (R≈W edges) and the temporal order relationships (time edges). Moreover, the **minor nodes** represent the static

properties of the transaction, such as the user balance, the transaction ID, and the chaincode number, and the dataflow edges link the minor nodes to the key nodes. The minor nodes

are interlinked by the control edges to indicate the internal relationships. The **hash nodes** indicate the hash value of each block, to model the read and write sets according to the corresponding position of the block, and they are connected with the minor nodes by the dataflow edges to represent the intra- and inter-block dependencies. The blockchain trans- action conflict graph depicted in Figure [5](#_bookmark47) is detailed as follows:

- - 1. _Read Nodes (Kr):_ Read sets of transactions (light blue). 2. _Write Nodes (Kw):_ Write sets of transactions (light green). 3. _Timestamp Nodes (Kt):_ Timestamps of the transaction (light coral). 4. _Minor Nodes:_ Static properties of a transaction such as transaction ID, user balance, and chaincode number (light grey). 5. _Hash Nodes_ (_H_ ) : Hash value in each block (light yellow).

The edges of different types of dependencies and rela- tionships that connect the nodes above are described subse- quently:

1. _R_ ≈ _W Edges:_ Represent read-write or write-read dependencies and connect the read nodes (Kr) to the write nodes (Kw) (blue).
2. _Time Edges_: Represent temporal relationships and con- nect the timestamps of transactions or time nodes (Kt) with each other (red).
3. _Dataflow Edges:_ Represent the data-flow dependencies among the minor nodes to the key nodes and the hash nodes (green).
4. _Control Edges:_ Represent the control dependencies between the minor nodes (purple).
5. _Kr-Kr Edges:_ Represent the read-read dependencies and connect the read nodes (Kr) with each other (cyan).
6. _Kw-Kw Edges:_ Represent the write-write dependencies and connect the write nodes (Kw) with each other (magenta).

For instance, if trans- action i writes to a data item that transaction j later reads or writes, a dependency is established, requiring an edge between them in the graph. For the proposed HFGIN model, key hyperparameters such as the number of hidden layers, the number of neurons in each layer, the learning rate for the optimizer, and the batch size for processing data were carefully selected based on their impact on the model’s accuracy and loss metrics. 1. _Learning Rate and Weight Decay:_ An essential aspect of the training process involves setting the learning rate and weight decay for the optimizer. For the proposed HFGIN model, an initial learning rate of 0.001 was cho- sen, combined with a weight decay of 0.01 to prevent overfitting by penalising large weights. The learning rate influences how quickly the model adapts to the problem, with a smaller value leading to slower con- vergence but potentially more precise model tuning.
2. _Optimizer and Learning Rate Scheduler:_ The AdamW optimizer was employed for its adaptive learning rate capabilities, which help in converging faster and more reliably in training deep neural networks.

Additionally, a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler was integrated to adjust the learning rate based on the vali- dation loss, ensuring that the model does not stall in its learning process and makes progress towards minimis- ing the loss.

1. _Batch Size and Epochs:_ The batch size determines how many examples the model sees before it updates the weight parameters. A smaller batch size was used to ensure more updates per epoch, potentially leading to a more efficient learning process. The model was set to train over 30 epochs, providing a balance between adequate learning time and computational efficiency. The epochs were determined to give the model enough iterations to learn from the entire dataset without over- fitting.

- 1. _MODEL EVALUATION_

The evaluation of the proposed HFGIN model over 30 epochs provides detailed insights into its performance, indicating substantial improvements in MVCC conflict detection within blockchain environments. The model’s evaluation, depicted through the careful analysis of accuracy metrics on both training and testing datasets, highlights its ability to learn efficiently and generalize, which is essential for model deployment in real-world settings. Starting with an initial training accuracy of 36.65% and test accuracy of 34.84%, the HFGIN model shows a commendable learning trajec- tory, with accuracies progressively climbing to 82.00% and 82.20%, respectively, by the end of the training period. Such convergence of training and testing accuracy suggests an ideal balance between learning the underlying data patterns and maintaining robustness against overfitting, which is a com- mon challenge in machine learning models. The precision of 0.8606 reflects a high reliability of the model’s positive con- flict predictions, indicating a strong specificity in identifying genuine conflicts. The recall of 0.7956 shows the model’s effectiveness in capturing a significant proportion of actual positive cases, essential for practical applications where miss- ing a conflict could be costly. Moreover, the F1 score of 0.8268 provides a balanced measure of precision and recall, indicating the model’s balanced capability in precision and sensitivity, which is essential for complex blockchain scenar- ios. Figure [9](#_bookmark64) illustrates a steady and consistent improvement in both training and testing accuracies, which aligns well with the descending trend observed in the loss values. The plot validates the quantitative analysis and visually communicates the model’s increasing confidence and capability in making accurate predictions as training progresses. The detailed eval- uation shows the model’s strengths in learning complexities of MVCC conflict data and its potential for broader applica- tions. Future research could focus on further optimizing the model’s architecture and training strategies, potentially incor- porating advanced techniques such as ensemble learning or deep reinforcement learning to further enhance the accuracies in blockchain conflict detection.

The GCN model’s test accuracy improves steadily but starts to plateau at around 0.7168, indicating potential limitations in its ability to generalize. In contrast, the GIN model outperforms GCN with a final test accuracy of 0.7895, exhibiting better generalization capabil- ities. The HFGIN model achieves the highest test accuracy, peaking at 0.8220. It indicates that HFGIN has robust gener- alization capabilities, making it the most effective of the three models in adapting to new and unseen data.

1. COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY

To assess the computational feasibility of deploying the HFGIN model within the Fabric execution pipeline, we con- ducted a profiling analysis focused on inference latency, CPU usage, and memory footprint during the early stage of conflict detection. As shown in Figure [14](#_bookmark70), HFGIN inference took approximately 5.8 milliseconds per transaction when exe- cuted on a GPU, and 17.2 milliseconds when running purely on CPU resources. Peak CPU utilization remained under 65%, while memory consumption stayed below 1.2 GB. These figures indicate that the model is lightweight enough for integration into the endorsement phase without intro- ducing excessive computational overhead. Furthermore, the

added inference stage leads to overall system-level improve- ments by filtering out conflict-prone transactions before they reach the more resource-intensive validation phase.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**FIGURE 14.** Computational efficiency of HFGIN.

To assess the practical feasibility of the proposed HFGIN model for early conflict detection in Hyperledger Fabric, it is essential to compare its performance with existing state-of- the-art MVCC conflict mitigation approaches. Fabric++ and FabricSharp as discussed earlier, are prominent frameworks

that have been widely adopted and studied for improving concurrency control in permissioned blockchains. Fabric++ introduces a reordering mechanism based on conflict graph cycle detection to handle intra-block conflicts, while Fab- ricSharp extends the approach to cover both intra- and

inter-block conflicts using snapshots and fine-grained con- currency control. However, both methods perform conflict detection and resolution after transaction endorsement and simulation, leading to resource wastage in case of late-stage invalidations.

In contrast, the proposed HFGIN model introduces an early-stage, predictive conflict detection strategy using graph neural networks. HFGIN enables pre-emptive identifica- tion of potentially conflicting transactions by modeling transactional dependencies and access patterns as struc- tured graphs during the endorsement phase. Since the smart contract simulates transactions execution at the endorse- ment stage resulting in data generation such as RW sets and timestamps, the transactional interactions graph can be constructed for preprocessing, therefore, detecting the transactions that are likely to fail validation. Such a proac- tive mechanism aims to reduce the number of transactions that proceed through costly endorsement, ordering, and validation phases only to be eventually aborted and resub-

mitted. Therefore, a comparative analysis against Fabric++ and FabricSharp is essential to evaluate whether the added

computational complexity of GNN-based inference is off- set by tangible improvements in throughput, latency, and conflict resolution efficiency. Figure [15](#_bookmark71) presents the through- put (TPS) and average transaction latency, respectively, for

HFGIN, Fabric++, and FabricSharp across block sizes ranging from 50 to 500 transactions. HFGIN consistently

demonstrates superior throughput, reaching a peak of

460 TPS, compared to 415 TPS for FabricSharp and 213 TPS for Fabric++. The performance gain is attributed to HFGIN’s early-stage conflict prediction, which significantly reduces the number of aborted or reordered transactions, thus enabling more efficient block utilization.

Similarly, the average latency for HFGIN is consistently lower, decreasing from approximately 3.1 seconds at 50 trans- actions to 2.4 seconds at 500 transactions. In comparison, FabricSharp records 2.54 seconds, and Fabric++ exhibits the highest latency at around 4.5 seconds for 500 transac-

tions. The results demonstrate the efficiency of HFGIN in preserving transaction integrity and reducing the cumulative processing time per block.

While neural network-based models inherently require additional computation specifically for graph construction and model inference, performance improvements in both latency and throughput demonstrate that these costs are justified and well-managed in the proposed architecture. HFGIN selectively applies intensive computation only to high-dependency transactions, allowing independent transac- tions to be executed in parallel, thereby optimizing resource usage and avoiding bottlenecks. Furthermore, early conflict detection helps minimize block space wastage, endorsement effort, and resubmission delays, which in turn contributes to better resource utilization across peer and ordering nodes. The selective application of HFGIN ensures that computa- tional costs are only incurred where necessary, enhancing system scalability without overloading network nodes.

The hybrid design of HFGIN combining conflict graph modeling with learned edge and node dependencies, makes it feasible for scaling to larger networks and workloads. Unlike Fabric++ and FabricSharp, which rely on hand- crafted dependency heuristics, HFGIN adapts dynamically

to the structure of the transactional graph and learns opti- mal conflict patterns over time making HFGIN a scalable and future-proof solution for high-throughput blockchain applications.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**FIGURE 15.** Comparative analysis of Fabric**++**, FabricSharp, and HFGIN in terms of throughput and latency across varying transaction block sizes.

1. SCALABILITY EVALUATION

To assess the scalability and operational feasibility of the proposed HFGIN model under large-scale blockchain workloads, we conducted an extended series of experi- ments using datasets with 3,000 and 5,000 transactions, in

addition to the baseline of 1,995. These experiments simu- lated increasing network load and complexity while preserv- ing conditions representative of real-world deployments. The number of user accounts was proportionally scaled to main- tain key diversity, preventing artificial conflict amplification due to repeated access to a narrow account range. The Zipfian skewness factor was fixed at 1.6 to reflect a moderately skewed access pattern that typifies a realistic mix of conflict and non-conflict transactions in Hyperledger Fabric-based systems.

As transaction volume increased, the corresponding trans- action conflict graph expanded in both node and edge count. The graph maintained sparsity, a common trait of blockchain workloads, which supports efficient GNN opera- tions. Additionally, performance metrics including memory consumption, graph construction time, training time, and inference latency were recorded to assess the model’s com- putational behavior.

The results shown in Table [3](#_bookmark72) indicate that while the graph structure becomes more complex with higher transaction volumes, HFGIN maintains linear scalability in both graph construction and model execution. Memory usage and train- ing times remain within reasonable operational limits for real-world blockchain deployment scenarios. The evalua- tion confirms that HFGIN remains computationally viable and efficient even at higher transaction scales. The model’s sparse graph structure, streamlined data representation, and batched GNN operations enable it to process thousands of transactions per block with minimal overhead, supporting enterprise-grade blockchain systems with responsive conflict management capabilities.

- 1. _GENERALIZATION EVALUATIONI UNDER VARYING SKEWNESS_

To validate the generalization capability of HFGIN beyond a fixed Zipfian skewness, we performed experiments across datasets generated with skewness values of 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, and

1.8. Each dataset contained approximately 2,000 transactions and was processed using the same model configuration to ensure comparability. The goal was to examine how HFGIN handles different levels of conflict density arising from vary- ing data access patterns.

As expected, lower skewness (e.g., 1.2) resulted in fewer MVCC_READ_CONFLICT transactions, while higher skewness (e.g., 1.8) led to a denser conflict graph due to intensified key reuse. Table [4](#_bookmark75) presents a summary of node and edge growth with increasing skewness, indicating how access locality influences the structural complexity of the conflict graph.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**FIGURE 16.** HFGIN model performance across Zipfian skewness levels.

The plot shown in Figure [16](#_bookmark73) shows how the HFGIN model performs across different levels of Zipfian skewness (1.2 to 1.8) in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The results highlight:

- 1. _Robustness:_ HFGIN maintains stable performance across varying skewness, peaking at Zipfian 1.6 with the best overall metrics.
  2. _Optimal Skewness:_ Zipfian 1.6 yields the highest F1- score and precision, validating its selection in the original experiments.
  3. _Justification:_ This supports the use of Zipfian 1.6 as a representative skew for conflict-prone environments while showing HFGIN’s generalization capability across distributions.

1. **SUMMARY**

The proposed HFGIN model introduces significant advance- ments in detecting MVCC conflicts within Hyperledger Fabric earlier than MVCC mechanism. The results obtained from the experimental analysis highlight the capability of HFGIN to outperform the baseline models, achieving a final accuracy of 82.20%, precision of 86.06%, recall of 79.56%, and an F1 score of 82.68%. The comparative analy- sis reveals that HFGIN reduces detection time and enhances the detection accuracy of MVCC conflicts significantly when compared to traditional GNNs such as GCN and GIN. The gradual and consistent improvement in epoch-based training accuracy, from 36.65% to an impressive score of 82.20%, demonstrates the model’s strong learning capabilities over time. Such improvement signifies the model’s effectiveness in handling real-world data variabilities and complexities inherent in blockchain transactions.

On a theoretical level, HFGIN’s innovative use of graph neural networks highlights a significant shift towards more

**TABLE 4.** Conflict graph metrics under varying zipfian skewness.

![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)

dynamic and adaptable blockchain technologies. HFGIN enhances the precision of conflict detection and also con- tributes to the broader understanding of blockchain dynamics by incorporating the complex dependencies and interac- tions within transaction data into a graph-based model. The enhanced detection capability is crucial for blockchain’s applicability in fields requiring high reliability and integrity of transaction processing, such as finance and healthcare.

Moreover, the implementation of HFGIN within blockchain systems such as Hyperledger Fabric could lead to a transformation in conflict management, promoting a shift from conventional methods to more effective, graph- based approaches especially when there a vast number of transactions received and processed per second. The poten- tial reduction in conflict-related failures could significantly increase system efficiency, providing a scalable solution that meets the growing demands of modern blockchain appli- cations worldwide. In addition to its predictive accuracy, HFGIN achieves a favorable balance between computational cost and performance, offering lower transaction latency and higher throughput than traditional reordering-based systems. The inference overhead introduced by HFGIN is modest and is effectively compensated by the reduction in failed transactions and improved system. The scalability evaluation further confirms the model’s ability to maintain performance across increasing transaction volumes and graph complex- ity. Its hybrid design ensures scalability across increasing transaction volumes by selectively applying inference to high-dependency transactions while parallelizing low-risk operations. Furthermore, generalization experiments con- ducted using datasets with varying Zipfian skewness values (1.2 to 1.8) show that HFGIN consistently maintains high accuracy and robustness, even under diverse contention intensities, reinforcing its applicability in heterogeneous enterprise environments. The HFGIN model is a significant advancement in blockchain management and contributes to theoretical perspectives on the way graph theory and machine learning can intersect to solve complex scientific problems. The implications of this research extend beyond technolog- ical enhancements, offering a foundation for future research into the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), blockchain technology and concurrency control methods, potentially transforming conflict management strategies across various sectors.

1. **CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK**

The HFGIN model introduces several advancements in the application of GNNs to blockchain technology, primarily in improving the accuracy and speed of MVCC conflict

detection. HFGIN facilitates a more reliable and efficient con- flict management process by effectively capturing the depen- dencies and interactions within the blockchain’s transactional data. This study contributes to the broader understanding of integrating machine learning techniques with blockchain technology, providing a scalable solution that enhances sys- tem efficiency and stability. The model also demonstrates strong computational efficiency, maintaining low inference latency and moderate memory usage, thereby validating its feasibility for integration during the endorsement phase. Scal- ability evaluations further confirm that HFGIN maintains linear growth in resource usage while processing larger trans- action volumes, proving its practicality for enterprise-scale blockchain deployments. Additionally, generalization testing under a range of Zipfian skewness settings (1.2–1.8) affirms the model’s robustness and adaptability to diverse transaction access patterns, further validating its generalization capa- bilities. Future work will extend this analysis by exploring additional benchmark workloads such as YCSB or real-world blockchain logs to further assess cross-domain adaptability.

While the results are promising, several avenues remain open for future research. Our future work will extend HFGIN further to enhance the conflict transactions resolution within order stage of EOV based on the generated graph for through- put and latency improvement in MVCC. Future work could also explore the integration of more complex graph-based neural network models to handle increasingly diverse and larger blockchain datasets. Enhancing the model’s scalabil- ity to accommodate larger networks without compromising performance would be crucial, particularly for enterprise- level applications. In addition, investigating the deployment of HFGIN in a real-world blockchain environment would provide valuable insights into its operational efficiency and practical challenges in an earlier stage of EOV architecture. It includes assessing the model’s responsiveness to dynamic changes in the network and its ability to adapt to new types of conflicts as blockchain technology evolves. Another potential area of research could focus on improving the inter- pretability of the model. Developing methods to visualize and interpret the decision-making process of the HFGIN model could increase trust and transparency that are essential factors in critical applications such as financial services and healthcare. Moreover, extending the HFGIN model to other types of blockchain architectures beyond Hyperledger Fabric, such as Ethereum or other permissioned or permissionless blockchain platforms, could broaden the model’s applica- bility and impact. It would involve adapting the network to different consensus mechanisms and transaction validation processes inherent in such diverse systems. As this area of

research continues to evolve, further innovations and research will clearly expand the capabilities and applications of GNNs within and beyond the blockchain domain.
